MIR: explicit execution and a validation boundary

MIR is the mid-level intermediate representation consumed by the interpreter and native backend, and carried in portable MIR images. It makes storage, evaluation order, calls, and control-flow edges explicit. It is not target assembly, not a second typechecker, and not a globally single-assignment IR.

See HIR for its semantic input and the overview for product routing.

Owners and entry points#

ResponsibilityPublic source
Core nodes and ID typesradix-mir/src/nodes.rs.
Traversal and successor enumerationvisit.rs.
HIR-to-MIR orchestrationradix-mir-lower/src/lower.rs, lower_analyzed_unit.
Validator and proof tokenvalidate/validator.rs.
Semantic validation metadatavalidate/context.rs, MirValidationContext.
Human-readable dumpdump.rs.
Package preparation/linkingradix-program/src/mir/driver.rs.

lower_analyzed_unit accepts an AnalyzedModuleApplicationView and MirLoweringOptions. It reads the analyzed unit immutably, clones its type arena and interner for lowering-owned extensions, collects context maps, lowers items and entry, and validates the result. The returned LoweredMirUnit owns its ValidatedMir token and carries auxiliary data such as monomorphizations, closure environments, generic templates, device metadata, and display tokens. Those facts are not all fields of MirProgram.

Errors are MirError values with an issue, primary span, and optional definition span. Unsupported HIR, missing semantic types, construction misuse, and invalid produced MIR are distinct causes even when reported through the same result channel. A successful semantic check does not imply that every consumer can lower or execute that program.

Program, function, and block#

The node definitions establish this shape:

  • MirProgram is a vector of MirFunction values. Function order gives stable rendering order; it is not the function-ID lookup table.
  • MirFunction has a MirFunctionId, optional source DefId and name, parameters, locals, temporaries, blocks, return and optional alternate-exit types, async/generator posture, shader stage, and span. A synthetic function may have no source definition; that does not determine its device role or visibility.
  • MirParam binds a typed parameter to a local slot. Its MirParamMode retains the parameter's access posture rather than making a backend rediscover it.
  • MirBlock has a MirBlockId, a sequence of statements, and exactly one MirTerminator. Block adjacency is not a control-flow edge.

IDs have separate namespaces: functions belong to a program; blocks, locals, temporaries, and value uses are interpreted in their function/block context. Do not cast an ID into a vector index and assume it identifies that element. MirFunctionIndex is the shared function lookup mechanism; MirProgram::allocate_function_id allocates max + 1 with checked overflow. MirFunction::block_by_id checks its dense fast path and falls back to a search, so sparse or reordered block IDs remain meaningful.

Places, operands, values, and statements#

These types are deliberately different:

TypeMeaning
MirPlaceStorage location: a local/temp base plus projections. A projection's validity and resulting type depend on validation metadata.
MirOperandReadable input: a place, temporary, earlier value ID, or constant.
MirValueA typed computation with a MirValueId, kind, type, and source span.
MirStatementAn operation in the current block; it does not choose a CFG successor.

MirValueKind includes operand, closure, unary/binary, option, and tensor-extent computations. MirStatementKind separates assignment from ordinary calls, runtime calls, and aggregate construction. Calls can write to an optional destination; constructors write an aggregate into a place. A value's ID is not the destination's storage ID.

Value ordering invariant: a MirOperand::Value is usable only after its defining assignment has been processed in the same block. In statement validation, the value map is cleared for each block and populated after validating the assigned value. Operand validation rejects an unknown value ID. This is not cross-block SSA dominance. To carry a result across control-flow edges, the representation uses addressable locals or temporaries, not an earlier block's value ID.

Locals and temporaries can be assigned repeatedly, so do not apply a global SSA optimization merely because a MirValueId exists. Producers must preserve evaluation sequencing, especially around effects, traps, and calls.

Terminators own control flow#

MirTerminatorKind includes:

  • Goto, Branch, and Switch, with explicit block IDs;
  • Return with an optional normal result;
  • ReturnError for the alternate-exit result;
  • TryCall with normal and error destinations/continuations;
  • Unreachable;
  • ReturnThread, a represented form that current structural validation rejects as pending lowering, rather than accepting it as ordinary return.

A failable call is a terminator because it selects a normal or error edge. An ordinary statement call must not silently discard that split. The validator checks successor existence, branch/return/call typing, and CFG structure; see stmt.rs. Use terminator_successors in visit.rs rather than maintaining a private, incomplete edge enumerator.

An illustrative control-flow sketch, not dump syntax or a Rust constructor:

entry:   compute condition; Branch -> then / else
then:    store chosen value into a result local; Goto join
else:    store alternate value into the same local; Goto join
join:    read the local; Return

A value ID computed only in then is not a legal operand in join merely because then precedes it in the block vector.

Type and metadata invariants#

MirType wraps a semantic TypeId and an optional MirLayoutId. Semantic identity comes from the matching type arena; a layout handle is not an inferred replacement type. Layout and physical representation helpers live in layout.rs.

MirValidationContext carries the type table, layout table, optional interner, function signatures, external identities, struct/variant field maps and order, closure environments, display facts, and other metadata needed to interpret those references. MirProgram alone is insufficient for all validation or execution. Empty metadata is valid only for a program that actually validates against it.

The validator is split by obligation:

ChecksImplementation
Program/function declarations, statement destinations, calls/returns, CFGstmt.rs.
Computations, operands, projections, call arguments, closuresvalue.rs.
Type validity and assignability helperstype.rs.
Aggregate fields and element representationaggregate.rs.
Runtime intrinsic signatures and operation constraintsintrinsic.rs.

This is a navigation summary, not a claim that validation proves all dynamic properties. Validation is a well-formedness/type/structural boundary. Runtime traps, target capability refusals, and host capability failures still exist.

The ValidatedMir proof token#

validate_program checks a borrowed program/context and returns success or MirValidationError values. ValidatedMir::new consumes the program and context, runs validation, and constructs the owned token. Public runner/native-emission entry points take this token instead of arbitrary bare MIR.

The token has no unrestricted mutable program accessor:

  • into_parts gives up the proof and returns the unvalidated parts.
  • patch_program consumes the token, permits a mutation, and returns a fresh token only after revalidation. On a patch or validation error the consumed program/context/token are not returned as validated state.
  • LoweredMirUnit::patch_program preserves this transition at the lowering carrier level.
  • detach / DetachedMir::attach support transferring already-validated data to a worker. Attachment preserves the proof; it is not a public unchecked constructor for arbitrary MIR.

The implementation is in validator.rs. Explicit role-aware constructors additionally enforce device composition obligations. A transformed program must not retain a token for an older program snapshot.

validated_mir_reject.rs constructs malformed programs to prove rejection, including missing block edges and invalid return forms. These tests are a useful companion to the positive lowering tests; acceptance alone cannot establish the rejection gate.

Linking, serialization, and execution#

Package linking#

Package MIR preparation composes analysis, import linking, unit lowering, merging, and validation. The linker, unit/merge lowering, and remapper preserve identities across independently allocated unit arenas. A numerical TypeId, Symbol, DefId, or function ID from one unit is not automatically valid in the merged program. Generic templates, closure metadata, display tokens, and device-origin facts must accompany the functions that need them.

Portable images#

radix-mir-fmir owns the FMIR schema and TOML-text/postcard-binary codecs. Package image assembly and reconstruction live in image.rs. Version/tag and wire integrity checks do not replace rebuilding the execution context and validating loaded MIR. Do not treat a text dump as the FMIR wire format.

Consumers#

  • radix-mir-runner interprets validated MIR. run_entry uses the default kernel-refusal policy. Other entry points carry explicit policies/limits; choosing a runner does not prove device support. Host is its process-effect seam, including diagnostic output and provider dispatch. Concrete hosts can expose or refuse capabilities.
  • radix-mir-clif accepts validated MIR for object or JIT emission and applies its own capability classification. runtime/clif supplies host runtime symbols; product build and JIT orchestration own linking or in-process launch. Structurally valid MIR can still be outside this backend's supported subset.

Debugging the boundary#

Use the narrowest observation that distinguishes the failure:

  1. faber check failing: investigate front-end analysis first.
  2. faber check --lower failing: inspect the structured lowering/validation issue and source span; no execution is needed to reproduce a bad CFG.
  3. faber mir showing wrong sequencing or edges: investigate the producer in radix-mir-lower and package transformations, not the runner.
  4. Correct MIR but wrong result: investigate runner operations, host effects, or the native lowering, with the same program/context as the failing run.
  5. Failure only after serialization or linking: compare reconstructed arenas, metadata, and validation, not just the printed function bodies.

These commands are investigative suggestions, not execution proofs for this manual. Full target coverage, device correctness, and runtime equivalence are not established by the structural contracts described here.
